body:
The decoder determines whether the code succeeds

All matrix equations for detectors and faults are over \(\mathbb F_2\). Q102 and Q66 are the \([[102,22,9]]\) memory and \([[66,4,10]]\) factory codes. A detector is a parity of measurement records expected to be zero without faults.

Q102 and Q66 checks return a syndrome, which must be converted into a correction. IonQ uses Ye, Wecker, and Delfosse's beam-search decoder in its logical-error estimates. A valid syndrome match can still give the wrong logical answer.

Distinguish detector parity from logical parity

Let binary vector \(e\) mark circuit faults. Columns of \(H\) specify the detector parities each fault flips; columns of \(A\) specify its logical-observable flips:

\[s=He,\quad\ell=Ae;\qquad H\hat e=s\ \text{is required, but success needs }A\hat e=Ae.\]

For independent fault probabilities \(p_j\), the most probable pattern minimizes

\[w(\hat e)=\sum_j\hat e_j\log\frac{1-p_j}{p_j}\quad\text{subject to }H\hat e=s.\]

Beam search heuristically explores patterns. An exact optimal quantum decoder would sum probabilities within each logical equivalence class.

Same syndrome, different logical class

In a three-bit repetition toy model, take \(H=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(A=(1,1,1)\), and \(p_j=0.1\).

Candidate\(H\hat e\)\(A\hat e\)Prior probability
010(1,1)10.081
101(1,1)00.009

The candidates differ by logical flip 111. Satisfying every check after correction does not distinguish them.

Belief propagation exchanges local evidence

Connect fault \(j\) to detector \(i\) when \(H_{ij}=1\). Let \(N(i),N(j)\) be neighbors of detector \(i\) and fault \(j\). \(D\) is a detector-to-fault message and \(E\) the reverse message, initialized to the prior. Start with log-likelihood \(\Lambda_j=\log((1-p_j)/p_j)\). Min-sum messages are

\[D_{i\to j}^{(t)}=(-1)^{s_i}\!\prod_{j'\in N(i)\setminus j}\operatorname{sign}E_{j'\to i}^{(t-1)}\;\min_{j'\in N(i)\setminus j}|E_{j'\to i}^{(t-1)}|,\qquad E_{j\to i}^{(t)}=\Lambda_j+\sum_{i'\in N(j)\setminus i}D_{i'\to j}^{(t)}.\]

Each detector demands the correct parity, with confidence limited by its least certain other neighbor. Updated belief \(\Lambda_j^{(t)}=\Lambda_j+\sum_{i\in N(j)}D_{i\to j}^{(t)}\) predicts zero when positive, one otherwise. Graph loops can make these beliefs oscillate.

Branch where evidence cancels

If ordinary BP fails, branch on the least reliable unfixed fault. Fixing \(e_j=v\) removes that variable and changes the residual syndrome to \(s\oplus vH_{:j}\). Each child resumes BP from its parent's messages; a beam retains up to \(B\) alternatives.

Here \(I\) counts iterations used for the score, \(B\) is beam width, and \(S_{\rm path}\) ranks one classical search path.

\[R_j=\left|\sum_{t=1}^{I}\Lambda_j^{(t)}\right|,\qquad S_{\rm path}=I^{-1}\sum_{j\ \mathrm{unfixed}}R_j.\]
Oscillation is uncertainty: beliefs \((+8,-8,+8,-8)\) give \(R_j=0\), despite a large final magnitude. Keep paths with larger \(S_{\rm path}\); this score is a heuristic, not a probability.

The multi-result variant chooses the least-weight valid candidate collected; the single-result variant stops at its first valid answer.

What enters IonQ's estimate

SettingValue
Beam width / search rounds32 / at most 10
Initial / subsequent BP iterations40 / 30 per round
Per-path iteration budget340, not total work over all paths

Pauli-only samples use Stim; loss/leakage uses the Walking Cat simulator. Fitting \(p_L(p)=p^5e^{a+bp+cp^2}\) and extrapolating to \(p=10^{-4}\) gives \(9.34\times10^{-12}\) (Q102) and \(2.63\times10^{-11}\) (Q66) per syndrome-extraction cycle. These are fitted extrapolations. Figure 7 does not disclose every sample count, seed, or fit uncertainty, and a decoder timing benchmark on another code does not establish this device's latency.

summary: A syndrome-compatible correction can still belong to the wrong logical class. Beam search retains several candidates when local evidence is ambiguous; its settings are part of the reported error model.
